items.definition: The local barometric pressure in inches of mercury (inHg) entered into the altimeter's Kollsman window before flight so the instrument reads accurate altitude above mean sea level.
items.analogy: Setting the altimeter is like zeroing a bathroom scale before weighing — without the correct reference baseline, every reading will be off by the same constant error.

items.definition: A flight instrument that measures and displays the rate of change of barometric altitude in feet per minute (fpm) by comparing the static pressure entering a chamber with a calibrated leak rate.
items.analogy: A VSI is like a pressure change detector — it doesn't read pressure, it reads how fast pressure is changing, which corresponds to how fast you're climbing or descending.

items.definition: An altimeter measures barometric altitude by sensing changes in static (atmospheric) pressure through an aneroid capsule; as altitude increases, pressure decreases, and the capsule expands, rotating gears to display altitude in feet or meters referenced to the set datum.
items.analogy: An altimeter is like a metal balloon inside a box — as you climb, outside pressure drops, the balloon expands, and a linked pointer shows how much it expanded, which corresponds to altitude.

items.definition: The FAA-standard 'Basic T' layout places four primary flight instruments in a T pattern: ASI (upper-left), AI (upper-center), ALT (upper-right), and heading indicator (lower-center).
items.analogy: The 'T' arrangement is designed so a pilot's eye naturally scans from the center (AI) outward to the wings (ASI left, ALT right) then down to the stem (HI bottom) — like reading a plus sign from the center out.

blocks.question: Why must the altimeter be set to the current local barometric pressure before flight?
choices: So the altimeter reads accurate altitude above sea level referenced to local atmospheric conditions
To prevent the static port from becoming blocked at altitude
To synchronize the altimeter with the air data computer
To set the transition altitude for pressurized aircraft
blocks.feedback: Without the correct local pressure setting, the altimeter references an incorrect baseline, causing altitude errors equal to approximately 1,000 ft per inch of mercury difference.

blocks.question: What does the Vertical Speed Indicator measure and how is it expressed?
choices: Absolute altitude above sea level, expressed in feet MSL
Dynamic pressure change, expressed in knots per minute
Rate of change of barometric altitude, expressed in feet per minute
Engine climb power setting, expressed in percent RPM
blocks.feedback: The VSI measures the rate at which static pressure is changing and converts this into a vertical rate reading in feet per minute — positive for climb, negative for descent.

blocks.question: How does a conventional altimeter determine and display barometric altitude?
choices: It measures ram pressure changes from the pitot tube and converts them to altitude
It calculates geometric altitude by triangulating GPS satellite signals
It senses static pressure through an aneroid capsule; pressure decreases with altitude, expanding the capsule to display altitude in feet
It receives digital altitude data from the ADC via a synchro motor system
blocks.feedback: A conventional aneroid altimeter senses static (atmospheric) pressure changes. Decreasing pressure at higher altitude expands the aneroid capsule, and mechanical linkages convert the expansion to an altitude reading.

blocks.question: What is the standard 'Basic T' arrangement of primary flight instruments?
choices: ASI upper-left, AI upper-center, ALT upper-right, HI lower-center
AI upper-left, ASI upper-center, ALT upper-right, HI lower-center
ASI upper-left, AI upper-center, HI upper-right, ALT lower-center
AI upper-left, HI upper-center, ASI upper-right, ALT lower-center
blocks.feedback: The FAA Basic T: ASI (airspeed indicator) at upper-left, AI (attitude indicator) at upper-center, ALT (altimeter) at upper-right, and DI/HI (heading indicator) at lower-center.
